title: The Adventure Doctrines

consts.name: dekEncounterTypeCount
consts.comment: the encounter taxonomy: twelve different types of encounters are described - combat, deception, delay, dilemma, event, guardian, interaction, obstacle, puzzle, skirmish, surprise, and trap - the categories not definitive, with considerable overlap (printed p. 36).

consts.name: dekLinkingMethodCount
consts.comment: the adventure-linking methods: five ways to turn separate adventures into a series - chained adventures, ripples in a pond, interlocking adventures, multi-layered adventures, and revisited adventures (printed pp. 40-42).

consts.name: dekCombatPlanElementCount
consts.comment: the combat-plan elements: a combat plan should consider five elements - attack power, mobility, organization, information, and terrain - with the planning depth riding the foe's intelligence and the encounter's plot importance (printed p. 43).

consts.name: dekSecretDoorSearchTurns
consts.comment: the delay economics: searching a 10' x 10' section of wall for a secret door requires a full turn (10 minutes) of game time, resolved in seconds of play - the model for delays that eat game time, not real time (printed p. 38).

consts.name: dekPolymorphSelfTurnsPerLevel
consts.comment: the polymorph self duration: two turns per caster level - the rules-springboard doctrine worked through the polymorphed lich example (printed p. 35).

consts.name: dekPolymorphLichTurns
consts.comment: the polymorphed lich: 60 turns (10 hours) at 30th level - the masquerade must renew the spell every 10 hours, the mumble to herself the neighbors noticed (printed p. 35).

consts.name: dekWorldTypeCount
consts.comment: the world types: three - the plane (infinitely large, no clear form or dimensions), the pocket dimension (a small discrete world attached to a parent, usually mirroring it, creatable artificially), and the demiplane (a discrete world floating in the Ethereal depths, creatable artificially, believed able to grow into full planes) (printed pp. 44-45).

consts.name: dekInnerPlaneCount
consts.comment: the inner-plane census: 18 inner planes - elemental, para-elemental, energy, and quasi-elemental; any undiscovered ones likely exist between known planes (printed p. 44).

consts.name: dekOuterPlaneCount
consts.comment: the outer-plane census: 17 known outer planes - sixteen forming the great ring with Concordant Opposition (the Outlands) in the middle; new ones would form between existing planes or as additional layers (printed p. 44).

consts.name: dekWorldAspectCount
consts.comment: the world aspects: four combine to define a world's unique reality - chronology, magic, technology, and environment (printed p. 45).

consts.name: dekWorldAspectMin
consts.comment: the world-rating floor: each aspect is rated on a scale ranging from 2 to 20, generated randomly with 2d10; the lower the rating, the weaker the aspect (printed p. 45).

consts.name: dekWorldAspectMax
consts.comment: the world-rating ceiling: 20 - ratings higher than 20 and lower than 2 are possible, but all known planes fall within these extremes (printed p. 45).

consts.name: dekWorldAspectTypicalLow
consts.comment: the typical campaign band, low end: ratings from 10 to 12 reflect conditions on typical AD&D campaign worlds - a 10 is weaker than a 12, but the difference is imperceptible to player characters (printed p. 45).

consts.name: dekWorldAspectTypicalHigh
consts.comment: the typical campaign band, high end: 12 - the typical-world ceiling; a world's rating is usually fixed, though some shift slowly over time without the residents realizing (printed p. 45).

bools.name: dekGoodAdventureDoctrine
bools.comment: the good-adventure checklist: begins with a hook, unfolds like a novel or short story plunging the characters into an ongoing web of activities, tests the skills of both player and character, contains plenty of excitement especially at beginning and end, and changes the world - always in a discernible way (printed p. 30).

bools.name: dekShowDontTell
bools.comment: the show-don't-tell rule: brief sensory descriptions for most scenes - colors, smells, textures, sounds - and the same for spells (the detect magic hues, the detect undead nausea, the fireball-or-delayed-blast ambiguity); sensory details control the mood (printed p. 32).

bools.name: dekPrepareDontOverplan
bools.comment: the prepare-don't-over-plan rule: high-level characters set their own agendas, so avoid work on encounters they might ignore; preparations mean hard data ready to hand - statistics, NPC personalities, treasure lists - not choreography; roll random events and rumors ahead of time and record them (printed p. 32).

bools.name: dekDontForceAction
bools.comment: the don't-force-the-action rule: treat the adventure as a story with an unwritten ending; build plots that stand up to PC tinkering; when something breaks the plan, put a backup plan into effect (the captured-villain worked example - the lie that still yields travel plans) (printed pp. 32-33).

bools.name: dekEncounterVariety
bools.comment: the encounter-variety rule: don't use just one type of encounter - offer a mix of challenges (combat, trick/trap, negotiation), the bulk of them the kind the players like best (printed p. 33).

bools.name: dekCombatVsCreativity
bools.comment: the combat-vs-creativity rule: don't encourage combat, encourage creativity - most combat rolls are moot for high-level characters; give problems that can't be solved through combat (the raging forest fire) and combats that require brain power (the hidden fire elemental) (printed p. 33).

bools.name: dekEnhanceDontInflate
bools.comment: the enhance-don't-inflate rule: resist bizarre new creatures with mind-boggling power, legions of high-level villains, or direct conflict with deities - enhancement challenges without overpowering (printed p. 33).

bools.name: dekGiftsVsRewards
bools.comment: the gifts-vs-rewards rule: a gift is anything the PCs haven't truly earned - the dragon trapped where it can't fly or breathe, the vorpal blade in a random hoard; a reward follows a long epic quest, and any battle with a really big dragon should be an epic conflict (printed pp. 33-34).

bools.name: dekMultipleThreats
bools.comment: the multiple-threats doctrine: a single source of threat generates only one type of challenge and coasts to a halt when overcome; multiple threats are flexible, resistant to PC successes, and offer variety (the kidnapper chase made rich with the rival party, the jungle, the tanar'ri) (printed p. 34).

bools.name: dekDontKillScare
bools.comment: the don't-kill-scare rule: grinding down high-level characters is monotonous - undermine confidence instead by attacking specific strengths (the silence 15' radius reminder, the antimagic shells, the heat metal and rust monster counters); undetectable foes make players assume the worst; lethal adventures drive retirement (printed p. 34).

bools.name: dekCharacterKnowledgeDoctrine
bools.comment: the character-knowledge doctrine: don't waste time on knowledge arguments - prepare reference materials for common knowledge and a rumor list passed around at the game's start; specialists know their own areas (the archmage and the old spell's new twist) (printed p. 34).

bools.name: dekRulesConsistency
bools.comment: the don't-ignore-the-rules doctrine: the rules define reality for the PCs as physics does for real folks - interpret them consistently or players lose their basis for meaningful decisions; the rules are a creative springboard (the polymorphed-lich worked example with its renewal schedule, the aura and the chilling touch, the thick gloves) (printed pp. 34-35).

bools.name: dekProactiveFoes
bools.comment: the proactive-foes rule: foes capable of challenging high-level adventurers make plans and actively implement them - they notice encroachment and act before too much damage is done; even stay-at-homes follow a personal agenda (printed p. 35).

bools.name: dekResponsiveFoes
bools.comment: the responsive-foes rule: PCs are a major disruption - plans already in motion should be dropped or altered to meet the situation; the keyed dungeon where occupants die room by room is the worst example - decide what goes on while the PCs are absent and make the locals react (printed p. 35).

bools.name: dekFailuresNotCatastrophic
bools.comment: the all-failures-not-catastrophic rule: not every situation should be all-or-nothing - if the PCs fail but survive, let the world change for the worse just a little and give them another chance; use failure to create further adventures (the dead king breaking the alliance, the deity's wrath) (printed p. 36).

bools.name: dekPlotDoctrine
bools.comment: the plot doctrine: a plot provides the unifying theme dealing with who, what, when, where, why, and how; it should arise from the campaign's structure, ride the player goals, and hook the characters through their personal goals or quirks; a good plot is flexible and decision-oriented - concentrate on what the players decide to do, not what their characters can accomplish (the worked newcomer example with its choice-preserving branches) (printed pp. 36-37).

bools.name: dekEncounterTaxonomyDoctrine
bools.comment: the encounter-type doctrines: combat needs a logical tactical plan; deception fails when overused or unvaried; delays eaten sparingly control magic by exhausting durations; the dilemma forces choices with apparent stakes; events advance plots and warn; guardians must survive a major offensive; interactions test communication (the sweet-toothed wizardess); obstacles combine with combat (the stone giants across the chasm); puzzles test the players, not the characters; the skirmish softens and probes; surprises used very sparingly; traps hinder rather than dose out damage, mindful of the hit-point spread (printed pp. 36-40).

bools.name: dekLinkingDoctrine
bools.comment: the linking doctrines: the chain needs only superficial links (clues, maps, NPC statements) and gives players freedom; the ripple uses consequences as springboards in a specified order or any order; the interlock nests one adventure inside another or follows the loose ends; the multi-layer peels toward a final conflict whose nature is hidden at the start; the revisited site keeps generating play (the thieves' guild, the flaring feud) (printed pp. 40-43).

bools.name: dekCombatPlanDoctrine
bools.comment: the combat-plan doctrines: plan less for unintelligent creatures and always carefully for major foes; concentrate attacks against as few enemies as possible - wounded creatures fight on - and disrupt spellcasters; nonlethal forms (charms, wrestling, entanglement, disarming) often limit counterattacks better than damage; mobility need not mean speed (walls, slow, transmute rock to mud; darkness and the clouds); one clever leader suffices for organization; fight on what the foe knows and can discover, and remember the PCs gather information too; terrain chooses the fight - cover for defenders, exposure for attackers, the castle doctrine (printed pp. 43-45).

bools.name: dekWorldHoppingDoctrine
bools.comment: the world-hopping doctrine: staging adventures on unfamiliar worlds keeps a high-level campaign fresh - even fairly weak creatures challenge when the spells and items act in unanticipated ways; the Ethereal connects the Prime with the Inner (travelers drift toward the Inner Planes or home, no Prime-to-Prime transit), the Astral connects the Prime to the Outer (and allows travel between Prime Material Worlds); both carry solid islands; the misconception corrected - only ONE Prime Material Plane, holding an infinity of crystal spheres (printed pp. 44-45).
